If you say: What is the connection of His words *min 'adhabin shadid* (from a severe punishment) to *al-wayl*? I say: because the meaning is that they wail from a severe punishment and cry out because of it, saying: "Woe to us!" like His words *da'aw hunalika thubura* ("they will call there for destruction").

*Unasun asaddu al-nasa bil-sayfi 'anhumu*
*sududu al-sawani fi unufi al-hawayimi*

It is a line of Dhu al-Rumma, which al-Farra' recited from him. It is said: *saddahu 'an kadhā*, and the dialect of Kalb: *asaddahu 'anhu* when he prevented him. So the verb *al-sudud* was used in place of *al-asdad*. *Al-sayafi* (with *fa*) means the winds, because they sweep the dust. It is also said that it is with *qaf*, the plural of *saq* or *saqiya*, which is above the irrigation channel. *Al-hawayim* means thirsty camels, because they circle around the water; the plural of *ha'im*. It is also applied to a bird which, when its thirst intensifies, circles around the water, and when it reaches it, its feathers fall and it drowns in it. Its plural is also *hawayim*. It may be intended here, or the mountains, because by their height they overlook from afar as if they were circling, or because birds circle above them, so attributing the action to them is metaphorical, since they are its locus. He says: a people who prevented people from themselves by the sword, as the winds prevent and strike the noses of the camels, or at the heights of the mountains, or like the water-carriers preventing other people's camels from their camels at watering, or like rivers, because their water is far, preventing thirsty camels or thirsty birds from drinking, because the birds fear drowning in it.

It is also narrated: *'an unufi al-hawayim* ("from the noses of the camels"). In it there is a comparison of the enemies to thirsty ones, and to the owners of swords, or of the swords to the winds, implicitly.

*Wa-yabghunaha 'iwajan* (and they seek to make it crooked): they seek for the way of God crookedness and deviation, and that they show people that it is a path deviating from the truth, not straight. The original is: *wa-yabghuna laha*, so the preposition was deleted and the verb was connected directly.

*Fi dalalin ba'id* (in far-off misguidance): that is, they strayed from the way of truth and stopped far short of it by stages.

If you say: what is the meaning of describing the misguidance as far? I say: it is a metaphorical attribution (*isnad majazi*), and the distance in reality belongs to the one who strays, because he is the one who distances himself from the path, so the attribute was applied to his action, as you say: *jadda jaddahu* (he strove his striving). It is also permissible that it means: "in misguidance having distance," or "in it there is distance," because the one who strays may stray from the path at a near place and at a far place.

Now, if you say: The Messenger of God ﷺ was not sent only to the Arabs; he was sent to all people, as He says: ﴿Say: O people, I am the messenger of God to you all﴾ [7:158], indeed to both humans and jinn (al-thaqalan), who speak different tongues. If the Arabs had no argument, then others would have an argument; and if others had no argument, then, had it been sent down in non-Arabic, the Arabs would likewise have had no argument.

I say: It is either sent down in all the tongues or in one of them. There is no need for it to be sent down in all tongues, because translation stands in for that and spares the lengthiness. It remains that it be sent down in a single tongue, and the most fitting of tongues is the tongue of the Messenger's people, because they are closest to him. When they understood him and clarified it, and it was transmitted from them and spread, the translations came to explain it and make it understood, as you see the situation and witness it in the substitution of translations in every non-Arab nation, along with what that entails of the agreement of peoples in distant lands, remote regions, [[His saying "remote regions" (al-aqtar al-mutanazahah) means extremely distant. Explained in al-Sihah. (ʿ)]] diverse nations and differing generations, upon one book, and their striving to learn its wording and learn its meanings, and what branches out from that of sublime benefits, and what multiplies in the exertion of souls and the toil of minds in it, of acts of nearness and obedience that lead to abundant reward. And because it is further from distortion and alteration, and safer from dispute and disagreement. And because, if it had been sent down in the tongues of both humans and jinn, all of them, despite their diversity and multiplicity, and it had been self-sufficient in the attribute of inimitability in each one of them, and the Arab Messenger had addressed every nation in its own tongue, just as he addressed his own nation of which he is part, reciting it to them as a miracle, that would have been a matter close to compulsion.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 14, verse 5:

"That bring out" (أَنْ أَخْرِجْ) is in the sense of "i.e., bring out" (بمعنى أى أخرج), because the sending (al-irsal) in it carries the sense of saying (al-qawl), as if it were said: "We sent him and said to him: bring out." It is also permissible that "an" (أن) be the particle (al-nasiba) that governs the verb in the subjunctive. It is appropriate that it be connected to an imperative verb because the purpose of connecting it is to join it to that which, together with it, is in the sense of a verbal noun (al-masdar), namely the verb and the imperative, and other than it is the same in being a verb. The evidence for the permissibility of "an" being the particle governing the verb is the saying: "He commanded him to (aw 'azza ilayhi bi-an) do," where they have placed the preposition (harf al-jarr) before it.

Likewise the estimate is: "that you bring out your people" and "remind them of the Days of Allah" (وَذَكِّرْهُمْ بِأَيَّامِ اللَّهِ), and warn them of His events that befell the nations before them: the people of Noah, 'Ad and Thamud. Among them are the Days of the Arabs for their wars and battles, such as the Day of Dhu Qar, the Day of al-Fijar, the Day of Qadah, and others, and this is the apparent meaning. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: His bounties and His trials.

Then the destruction of the generations is "a sign for every patient, grateful one" (لِكُلِّ صَبَّارٍ شَكُورٍ), who endures the trial of Allah and gives thanks for His blessings. So when he hears of what Allah sent down of trial upon the nations, or what He poured out upon them of blessings, he is alerted to what is obligatory upon him of patience and gratitude, and takes heed.

It has been said: He intended every believer, because gratitude and patience are among their characteristics, as an alert to them.

The phrase إِذْ أَنْجاكُمْ is a time adverb (ẓarf) modifying "the blessing" (al-ni'mah) in the sense of "the bestowal" (al-in'am), meaning His bestowal upon you at that time. If you ask whether it could be governed by عَلَيْكُمْ ("upon you"), the answer is that it has two possibilities. Either عَلَيْكُمْ is a complement (ṣilah) of al-ni'mah in the sense of al-in'am, or it is not a complement, if by al-ni'mah you mean "the gift." If it is a complement, it does not govern إِذْ. If it is not a complement, meaning "remember the blessing of God that is settled upon you," then it governs it. The difference between the two readings becomes clear when you say "the blessing of God upon you." If you make it a complement, the sentence is not complete until you add "overflowing" or something similar. Otherwise, it is a complete sentence. It is also permissible for إِذْ to be a substitute (badal) for نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ, meaning "remember the time of His delivering you." This is substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal).

If you ask: in Surat al-Baqarah it is ﴿يُذَبِّحُونَ﴾, in al-A'raf it is ﴿يُقَتِّلُونَ﴾, and here it is ﴿وَيُذَبِّحُونَ﴾ with the waw, what is the difference? The answer is that where the waw is omitted, slaughtering (al-tadhbih) is presented as an explanation and clarification of the torment. Where the waw is affirmed, slaughtering is treated as one of the kinds of torment, and it is added to it as a clear addition, as if it were a different kind.

If you ask: how could the deeds of the people of Pharaoh be a trial (balaʾ) from their Lord? The answer is that it was their empowerment and their being granted respite, until they did what they did as a trial from God. Another explanation is that this refers to the deliverance, which is a great trial, and trial can be a test through blessing and through affliction alike. God the Exalted says: ﴿وَنَبْلُوكُمْ بِالشَّرِّ وَالْخَيْرِ فِتْنَةً﴾ ("And We test you with evil and with good as a trial"). Zuhayr said:

So He tested them both with the best of tests, the test that tests.

[[Earlier explanation of this line appears on page 208 of this volume; consult it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

﴿وَإِذْ تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكُمْ﴾ is part of what Musa said to his people. Its position in the grammar (nasb, accusative) is by way of 'atf (conjunction) to His words ﴿نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾, as if it had been said: "And when Musa said to his people, 'Remember God's blessing upon you,' and remember when your Lord proclaimed..."

The meaning of ﴿تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكُمْ﴾ is: "Your Lord proclaimed" (adhina rabbukum). The relation between تأذن (ta'adhdhana) and أذن (adhana) is like that of توعد (tawaʿada) and أوعد (awʿada), or تفضل (tafaddala) and أفضل (afdala). In the form تفعل (tafaʿʿala) there must be an added meaning not present in أفعل (afʿala), as if it had been said: "Your Lord proclaimed with an emphatic proclamation, by which doubts are dispelled and suspicions removed." The meaning is: "And when your Lord proclaimed, and said, ﴿لَئِنْ شَكَرْتُمْ﴾ ('If you are thankful...')." Or تأذن is treated as if it were قال (qala, "said"), because it is a kind of speech.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "And when your Lord said, 'If you are thankful...'" That is, "If you are thankful, O Children of Israel, for what He has bestowed upon you of the blessing of deliverance and other blessings, with sincere faith and righteous deeds, ﴿لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ﴾ ('I will surely increase you'), blessing upon blessing, and ﴿لَأُضَاعِفَنَّ لَكُمْ مَا آتَيْتُكُمْ﴾ ('I will surely multiply for you what I have given you'). ﴿وَلَئِنْ كَفَرْتُمْ﴾ ('But if you are ungrateful'), and reject and disdain [[قوله «وغمطتم ما أنعمت به عليكم» في الصحاح «غمط الشيء» بطره وحقره. (ع)]] what I have bestowed upon you, ﴿إِنَّ عَذَابِي لَشَدِيدٌ﴾ ('My punishment is indeed severe') for whoever disbelieves My blessing."

Moses said: If you disbelieve, you and all the people together, then you have only harmed yourselves and deprived yourselves of the good which you cannot do without and to which you are in need. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Free of need from your gratitude, Praiseworthy﴾ — deserving of praise for the abundance of His blessings and favours, even if those who praise Him do not praise Him.

The clause ﴿and those after them, none knows them but Allah﴾ is a nominal sentence (jumlah min mubtada' wa khabar; a subject and predicate, mubtada' and khabar), and it occurs as a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ). Alternatively, ﴿those after them﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿the people of Noah﴾. The phrase ﴿none knows them but Allah﴾ is itself a parenthetical clause. The meaning is that they are so numerous that only Allah knows their number. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that between ʿAdnan and Ismaʿil there were thirty fathers whom no one knows. Ibn Masʿud, whenever he recited this verse, would say: "The genealogists have lied," meaning that they claim knowledge of lineages, whereas Allah has denied that knowledge to His servants.

﴿They put their hands into their mouths﴾, that is, they bit them out of rage and vexation at what the messengers had brought. [Mahmud said: "Its meaning is that they bit them out of rage and vexation at what the messengers had brought…" etc. Ahmad said: The strongest of these interpretations is this one, which the author (al-Musannif) drew attention to as having special strength. It is so because their despairing the messengers of faith, in word and deed, by placing the hand in the mouth, is the fitting expression for their envy in disbelief. Introducing the statement with the emphatic particle, confronting the messengers with the second-person pronouns, and repeating that is an intensification of emphasis. The context does not suit laughter, nor rage, nor silencing the messengers as it suits despairing them of being accepted. Do you not see that when they repeated the words to the messengers and did not object to their returning to dispute, this shows that they had not silenced them at first, nor was that their aim, and Allah knows best.]

It is like His saying: ﴿they bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾. Or it is laughter and mockery, like one overcome by laughter who places his hand on his mouth. Or they pointed with their hands to their tongues, and to what their tongues uttered of their saying: ﴿Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾, meaning: this is our answer to you, and we have nothing other than it, in despair of their assent. Do you not see His saying: ﴿they put their hands into their mouths and said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾? This is a strong view. Or they placed them on their mouths, saying to the prophets: "Close your mouths and be silent." Or they put them back into the mouths of the prophets, pointing to them to be silent. Or they placed them on their mouths to silence them and not allow them to speak.

It is said: "al-Aydi" is the plural of yad (hand), which here means blessing (niʿmah), in the sense of al-Ayadi (blessings). That is: they returned the blessings of the prophets, which are the most excellent blessings, namely their admonitions and counsels and the laws and signs revealed to them, into their mouths, because when they denied them and did not accept them, it was as if they had returned them into their mouths and sent them back to where they had come from. This is in the manner of a figure of speech (ʿalā ṭarīq al-mathal).

﴿what you call us to﴾, namely faith in Allah. It is recited as "tadʿūnā" with the nun assimilated (idghām). ﴿disquieting﴾ (murīb): causing doubt (fī al-rība), or possessing doubt (dhū rība), from arābahu (he caused him doubt), and arāba al-rajul (the man became doubtful). It is the unease of the soul and its failure to be at rest regarding a matter.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 14, verse 10:

"Is there doubt about Allah?" The interrogative particle of denial (hamzat al-inkar) has been placed before the adverbial phrase (al-zarf), because the discussion is not about doubt itself but about that which is doubted, and that it does not admit of doubt, given the clarity of the proofs and their testimony to it. ﴿He calls you that He may forgive you some of your sins﴾: that is, He calls you to faith so that He may forgive you, or He calls you for the sake of forgiveness, like the saying: "I called him so that he would help me," and "I called him so that he would eat with me." And he (the poet) said:

"I called Miswar when calamity befell me, so he answered, then answered again, the two hands of Miswar."

[[By a Bedouin of the Banu Asad. "Labbay" means "answered," and Ibn Habib wrote it with an alif though it is from the ya' root, to distinguish it from the dual that follows it. "Labbay" is among the words that are obligatorily attached to a pronoun, and its being attached to a noun, as here, is anomalous. It derives from "labba bi-l-makan," meaning he stayed in the place. The intended meaning is a constant answering, answer after answer, not merely two. It is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar) governed by a deleted verb. This is the view of Sibawayh. Yunus claimed that it is a singular defective noun whose alif was changed to ya' when attached to a pronoun, like "ladaa" and "ala." Sibawayh refuted him by saying that if this were so, its alif would not have changed to ya' when attached to a noun, like "ladaa" and "ala"; but since they attached it to a noun, they changed it to ya', as in the verse.]] He says: I called Miswar when calamity befell me, so he answered me, then answered again with his two hands; that is, Allah answered his prayer after an answer. The two hands are mentioned because they are raised during supplication, so they are as if they were the ones answering, or because his help was achieved through them, which indicates that he rescued him. It was also said: he called him so that he would pay the blood-money on his behalf, so he answered him, and he mentioned his hands because he gave with them. It was said that this was a custom of the Arabs, and it was forbidden. It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "If one of you calls his brother and he says, 'Labbayk,' let him not say, 'Labba yadayk,' but let him say, 'May Allah answer you with what you love.'"

But if you ask: what is the meaning of the partitive in His words "some of your sins"? I say: I know of it coming in this form only in addressing the disbelievers, such as His words: ﴿Fear Him and obey me; He will forgive you some of your sins﴾, ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of Allah and believe in Him; He will forgive you some of your sins﴾. And in addressing the believers He said: ﴿Shall I direct you to a commerce that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ up to His words ﴿He will forgive you your sins﴾, and other instances that induction will reveal to you. This was for the sake of distinguishing between the two addresses, and so that the two groups would not be equated in the promise. It was also said: what is meant is that He forgives them what lies between them and Allah, unlike what lies between them and the servants, such as wrongs and the like. ﴿And defer you to a specified term﴾: to a time that Allah has named and whose extent He has determined, which He will let you reach if you believe, and otherwise He will hasten your destruction before that time. ﴿They said: You are only mortals like us﴾: there is no superiority between us and you, nor any superiority for you over us. ﴿So why do you wish to be preferred over us?﴾ [[His words resumed. He said: "Their words, 'You are only mortals like us,' mean: why are you singled out for prophethood over us? Had Allah sent messengers to mankind, He would have made them from a kind superior to them, namely the angels."]] Ahmad said: Because of his fervor in defending his belief that the angels are superior to human messengers, he seeks help until he attributes to the disbelievers the belief that the angels are superior to the Messenger, in the manner of the Qadariyya, since he claims that this is a matter fixed in human nature and known by necessity. And Allah is the Granter of success. ﴿Unless you bring us a clear authority﴾: a manifest proof. Their messengers had already come to them with clear signs and proofs, and they only meant by "clear authority" a sign they had demanded out of obstinacy and stubbornness.

[[Al-Zamakhshari's words "...and He would have made them from a kind superior to them, namely the angels" are according to the Mu'tazila's doctrine; but according to the Ahl al-Sunna, some humans are superior. (Gloss)]]

The Arabic text is a passage from al-Zamakhshari's al-Kashshaf, and I'll translate it faithfully.

"They are only human beings like you": this is a concession to their words, and that they are human like them, meaning that they are alike in humanity alone. As for beyond that, they were not like them. But they did not mention their own superiority out of humility, and they confined themselves to their statement: ﴿But God bestows His favour upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾ with prophethood, for He knew that He would not single them out with that honour except that they were worthy of being singled out for it, by qualities in them with which they had set themselves apart from their fellow men. ﴿Except by the permission of God﴾: they meant that bringing the sign you have proposed is not up to us and not within our power, and that it is only a matter that depends on the will of God. ﴿And upon God let the believers put their trust﴾: this is a command from them to all believers to rely upon God, and by it they primarily intended themselves and commanded themselves to do so, as if they said: it is our right to rely upon God in bearing your opposition and enmity and what befalls us from you. Do you not see His saying ﴿And why should we not put our trust in God﴾, meaning: what excuse do we have for not relying upon Him ﴿when He has guided us﴾ to our ways, and has done to us what necessitates our reliance upon Him, namely granting us success in being guided, each of us, to the path that he must follow in religion? If you ask: how did He repeat the command to rely [[Mahmud said: "If you ask, how did He repeat that after His saying ﴿And upon God let the believers put their trust﴾ ... etc." Ahmad said: With this he departs from the category of "whoever kills an enemy, he shall have his spoils." And God knows best.]]? I say: the first is for initiating reliance, and His saying ﴿So let those who rely upon Him put their trust﴾ means: let those who rely upon God remain steadfast in the reliance they have newly developed, and their intention toward themselves, as previously stated.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 14, verse 12–14:

﴿Surely we will expel you,﴾ or ﴿you shall return﴾ to our religion, meaning that one of the two matters will certainly happen: either your expulsion or your return, they swearing oaths upon that. [[His saying "swearing oaths" is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "said". The wording of al-Nasafi is "and they swore". (Ed.)]] If you say: it is as though they were upon their religion, such that they would "return" to it? I say: God forbid. Rather, "return" here carries the sense of "becoming", which is very common in the speech of the Arabs, so commonly that you hardly hear them use "ṣāra" (became), but rather "ʿāda": "I do not see him returning (ʿāda) to speak to me," "there is no property returning (ʿāda) to so-and-so." Or they addressed it to every messenger and whoever believed in him, the plural being given precedence over the singular in address. ﴿We will surely destroy the wrongdoers﴾ is a quoted speech that requires the implication of a saying, or the revelation (īḥāʾ) is treated as speech, since it is a kind of speech. Abū Ḥaywa recited "liyuhlikanna" and "liyuskinannakum" with the yāʾ, taking into account "awḥā" (revealed) and that its wording is in the third person, similar to your saying: "Zayd swore that he would certainly go out" and "I will certainly go out."

The intended meaning of "the land" is the land of the wrongdoers and their dwellings, similar to ﴿And We caused the people who were oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the land﴾ and ﴿and made you inherit their land and their dwellings﴾. It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever harms his neighbour, God will make him inherit his house." [[I have not found it.]] I witnessed this within a recent period: I had a maternal uncle who was wronged by a great man of the village to which I belong, and who harmed me on his account. That great man died, and God gave me possession of his estate. One day I looked at my maternal cousins moving about in it, entering its houses, going out, commanding and forbidding, and I remembered the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and I related it to them, and we prostrated in thanks to God.

﴿That﴾ refers to what God has decreed of destroying the wrongdoers and settling the believers in their dwellings; that is, that matter is true. ﴿For whoever fears My standing﴾, meaning My station, which is the station of reckoning, since it is the station of God where His servants stand on the Day of Resurrection. Or it is on the basis of the insertion of "maqām" as an intensifier. It has been said: "he feared my standing over him and my preserving of his deeds." The meaning is that this is true for the righteous, as in His saying: ﴿and the final outcome is for the righteous﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 14, verse 15–17:

﴿And they sought victory,﴾ that is, they sought help from God against their enemies. ﴿If you seek a victory, then there has come to you the victory.﴾ Or: they sought judgment (istihkam) from God, and asked Him to decide between them. It is from al-fataha (the judgment), which is al-hukuma (the ruling), like His saying, ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth.﴾ It is coordinated with ﴿So He revealed to them﴾ (fa-awha ila-himm). And it is read: ﴿wa-istaftahu﴾ (and seek victory!), in the imperative form. Its coordination with ﴿we will surely destroy﴾ (la-nuhlikanna) means: their Lord revealed to them and said to them, "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers," and said to them, "Seek victory!" ﴿And every obstinate tyrant failed,﴾ meaning: they were helped, succeeded and prevailed, while ﴿every obstinate tyrant failed﴾ — and they are their people. It is also said: the disbelievers sought victory against the messengers, thinking that they were upon the truth and the messengers upon falsehood, and ﴿every obstinate tyrant failed﴾ among them, and did not succeed by his seeking victory. ﴿Behind him﴾ means before him. He said:

*Perhaps the distress in which you have been evening*
*Will have behind it a near relief.*

This is by Hadba ibn Khashram al-Udhri, also narrated as "Kharshum." He was imprisoned for execution. Al-tarq (ta'riq) means keeping awake at night, and al-iktiʼab means being broken and the color changing from grief; al-kaʼaba is likewise. Abu Numayr was a friend of his; he visited him in prison and grieved over him. Mahlan is a verbal noun substituted for the verb's utterance. Khayr al-qawl is a parenthetical clause within the speech. Al-lubb means intellect. ʻAsa al-karb is the completion of the speech. It is also narrated as "amsaytu," with damma and fatha. Al-Jawhari said that "wara'" comes in the sense of "behind" and may also come in the sense of "in front," so it is among the words with opposite meanings, because what is behind a person, concealing him from himself or from others, can only be behind him, so it was frequent in that sense. Or it is the place of concealment in general, and it is mostly behind. The subject of "yakun" is the pronoun referring to the distress, and "warā'ahu" is related to an omitted predicate of "yakun," and "faraj" is the agent of the adverbial phrase. It is permissible that "faraj" is the subject and "warā'ahu" is related to an omitted predicate of it, and the clause is the predicate of "yakun"; the omitted predicate must be a complete (tamm) verb, not a incomplete (naqis) one, lest it require yet another omitted element, so the estimation would regress. "Faraj" was not made the nominative of "yakun," because the predicate of the verbs of approximation does not raise a noun foreign to its subject. The clause "yakun" is the predicate of "laysa," and omitting "an" from its predicate is rare, meaning: perhaps relief will come after distress.

This describes his condition while in this world, since he is set up for Hell, so it is as if it were before him while he stands on its brink. Or it describes his condition in the Hereafter, when he is raised and made to stand. If you ask: on what is ﴿and he is given to drink﴾ (wa-yusqa) coordinated? I say: it is coordinated with an omitted element whose estimate is: "Behind him is Hell, into which he will be cast and given to drink of water of pus," as if it were the most severe of its torments. So it was singled out for mention along with His saying, ﴿and death comes to him from every place, yet he is not dead.﴾ If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying, ﴿of water of pus﴾? I say: "pus" is an explanatory apposition to "water." He said ﴿he is given to drink of water﴾, leaving it vague, then clarified it with ﴿pus﴾, which is what flows from the skins of the people of the Fire. ﴿He gulps it down﴾ means he forces himself to swallow it, ﴿and scarcely can he swallow it﴾: "kada" is used for emphasis, meaning he almost cannot swallow it, so how could he swallow it, like His saying, ﴿he could hardly see it﴾, meaning he came nowhere near seeing it, so how would he see it? ﴿Death comes to him from every place﴾, as if the causes and kinds of death had all gathered against him [[His saying "qad tu'allabat 'alayhi" means gathered together. Stated in al-Sihah. (ʻ)]] and surrounded him from all directions, to make dreadful what afflicts him of pain. It is said: ﴿from every place﴾ means from his body, even from the tip of his toe. It is said: from the root of every hair. ﴿And behind him is a severe torment﴾, meaning at every time he confronts, he meets a torment harsher and more severe than what came before. It is narrated from al-Fudayl: it is the cutting off of breaths and their confinement within the bodies. It is possible that the people of Makkah sought victory, meaning they sought rain (al-fath being rain), in the years of drought that were sent upon them through the supplication of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they were not given water; so He, glorified is He, mentioned this, and that He frustrated the hope of every obstinate tyrant, and that in Hell he is given to drink another water instead of his drink, namely the pus of the people of the Fire. ﴿And they sought victory﴾, according to this interpretation, is a new, separate statement, disconnected from the account of the messengers and their peoples.

Al-tarq (ta'riq) means keeping awake at night, and al-iktiʼab means being broken and the color changing from grief; al-kaʼaba is likewise. Abu Numayr was a friend of his; he visited him in prison and grieved over him. Mahlan is a verbal noun substituted for the verb's utterance. Khayr al-qawl is a parenthetical clause within the speech. Al-lubb means intellect. ʻAsa al-karb is the completion of the speech. It is also narrated as "amsaytu," with damma and fatha. Al-Jawhari said that "wara'" comes in the sense of "behind" and may also come in the sense of "in front," so it is among the words with opposite meanings, because what is behind a person, concealing him from himself or from others, can only be behind him, so it was frequent in that sense. Or it is the place of concealment in general, and it is mostly behind. The subject of "yakun" is the pronoun referring to the distress, and "warā'ahu" is related to an omitted predicate of "yakun," and "faraj" is the agent of the adverbial phrase. It is permissible that "faraj" is the subject and "warā'ahu" is related to an omitted predicate of it, and the clause is the predicate of "yakun"; the omitted predicate must be a complete (tamm) verb, not a incomplete (naqis) one, lest it require yet another omitted element, so the estimation would regress. "Faraj" was not made the nominative of "yakun," because the predicate of the verbs of approximation does not raise a noun foreign to its subject. The clause "yakun" is the predicate of "laysa," and omitting "an" from its predicate is rare, meaning: perhaps relief will come after distress.

This describes his condition while in this world, since he is set up for Hell, so it is as if it were before him while he stands on its brink. Or it describes his condition in the Hereafter, when he is raised and made to stand. If you ask: on what is ﴿and he is given to drink﴾ (wa-yusqa) coordinated? I say: it is coordinated with an omitted element whose estimate is: "Behind him is Hell, into which he will be cast and given to drink of water of pus," as if it were the most severe of its torments. So it was singled out for mention along with His saying, ﴿and death comes to him from every place, yet he is not dead.﴾ If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying, ﴿of water of pus﴾? I say: "pus" is an explanatory apposition to "water." He said ﴿he is given to drink of water﴾, leaving it vague, then clarified it with ﴿pus﴾, which is what flows from the skins of the people of the Fire. ﴿He gulps it down﴾ means he forces himself to swallow it, ﴿and scarcely can he swallow it﴾: "kada" is used for emphasis, meaning he almost cannot swallow it, so how could he swallow it, like His saying, ﴿he could hardly see it﴾, meaning he came nowhere near seeing it, so how would he see it? ﴿Death comes to him from every place﴾, as if the causes and kinds of death had all gathered against him [[His saying "qad tu'allabat 'alayhi" means gathered together. Stated in al-Sihah. (ʻ)]] and surrounded him from all directions, to make dreadful what afflicts him of pain. It is said: ﴿from every place﴾ means from his body, even from the tip of his toe. It is said: from the root of every hair. ﴿And behind him is a severe torment﴾, meaning at every time he confronts, he meets a torment harsher and more severe than what came before. It is narrated from al-Fudayl: it is the cutting off of breaths and their confinement within the bodies. It is possible that the people of Makkah sought victory, meaning they sought rain (al-fath being rain), in the years of drought that were sent upon them through the supplication of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they were not given water; so He, glorified is He, mentioned this, and that He frustrated the hope of every obstinate tyrant, and that in Hell he is given to drink another water instead of his drink, namely the pus of the people of the Fire. ﴿And they sought victory﴾, according to this interpretation, is a new, separate statement, disconnected from the account of the messengers and their peoples.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 14, verse 15–17:

﴿And they sought victory,﴾ that is, they sought help from God against their enemies. ﴿If you seek a victory, then there has come to you the victory.﴾ Or: they sought judgment (istihkam) from God, and asked Him to decide between them. It is from al-fataha (the judgment), which is al-hukuma (the ruling), like His saying, ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth.﴾ It is coordinated with ﴿So He revealed to them﴾ (fa-awha ila-himm). And it is read: ﴿wa-istaftahu﴾ (and seek victory!), in the imperative form. Its coordination with ﴿we will surely destroy﴾ (la-nuhlikanna) means: their Lord revealed to them and said to them, "We will surely destroy the wrongdoers," and said to them, "Seek victory!" ﴿And every obstinate tyrant failed,﴾ meaning: they were helped, succeeded and prevailed, while ﴿every obstinate tyrant failed﴾ — and they are their people. It is also said: the disbelievers sought victory against the messengers, thinking that they were upon the truth and the messengers upon falsehood, and ﴿every obstinate tyrant failed﴾ among them, and did not succeed by his seeking victory. ﴿Behind him﴾ means before him. He said:

It is the subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, according to Sibawayh. Its estimated form is: "And among what is recounted to you is the example of those who disbelieve in their Lord." The word *mathal* (example) is used figuratively for an attribute that is strange.

His saying, ﴿their deeds are like ashes﴾, is a resumptive sentence (*jumla mustanafa*), on the presumption of a questioner who asks: "What is their example?" So it is said: "Their deeds are like ashes."

It is permissible that the meaning be: the example of the deeds of those who disbelieve in their Lord. Or this sentence is the predicate of the subject, meaning: the attribute of those who disbelieve is that their deeds are like ashes, as in your saying, "The attribute of Zayd is that his honour is protected and his wealth is spent freely." Or ﴿their deeds﴾ is an apposition (*badal*) to ﴿the example of those who disbelieve﴾, on the estimate: "the example of their deeds," and ﴿like ashes﴾ is the predicate.

It is also read ﴿al-riyah﴾ (the winds) ﴿in a stormy day﴾. He attributed the stormy quality (*'asif*) to the day, while it belongs to what is in it, namely the wind or the winds, as in your saying "a rainy day" and "a calm night." Rather, the calm (*sukur*) belongs to its wind. [[His saying "the calm belongs to its wind": in al-Sihah: *sakarat al-rih*, *yaskuru sukuran*, meaning the wind became calm after blowing. (ع)]]

It is also read: ﴿in a stormy day﴾ with the genitive construction (*idafa*).

The deeds of the disbelievers are the noble acts they performed, such as maintaining ties of kinship, freeing slaves, ransoming captives, slaughtering camels for guests, relieving the distressed, generosity, and other good works. He likened their being nullified and gone, becoming ﴿scattered dust﴾, because they were built on no foundation of knowledge of God and belief in Him, and because they were not for His sake: they are like ashes that a stormy wind has scattered.

﴿They have no power over anything of what they earned on the Day of Resurrection﴾, i.e., they see no trace of reward from it, just as nothing can be obtained from ashes scattered by the wind.

﴿That is the far-gone error﴾ indicates how far their error is from the path of truth, or from reward.

﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾: with wisdom, the correct purpose, and a great matter. He did not create them in vain, nor out of desire. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning: He created them with wisdom and the correct purpose... etc." Ahmad said: This is from his hidden Mu'tazilism, and similar examples have preceded.]]

Also read: ﴿Creator of the heavens and the earth﴾, ﴿if He wills, He will remove you﴾. That is, He is able to annihilate people and create others in their place, of the same form or of a different form, informing [them] of His power to annihilate what exists and to bring into existence what does not, [and] that He can determine one thing and its opposite. ﴿And that is not difficult for Allah﴾, meaning not impossible for Him, but rather easy and simple for Him. [[His words resume. He said: its meaning is "and that is not difficult for Allah," that is, easy for Him, because He is powerful by His very essence, etc. Ahmad said: this is an explicit Mu'tazilite doctrine (i'tizal) that they cloak in its presentation. How abominable is his saying about God, exalted is His majesty. The motive of it [in him] has gained the upper hand and the deterrent has been overcome. How far it is from the hearing of the verifiers and gnostics who know the courtesies due to God Most High and what is owed to His majesty. What is in it has already been mentioned in sufficient measure.]] Because He is powerful in His essence, there is no restriction on Him regarding one object over another. So when the motive toward something is pure for Him and the deterrent is absent, it comes into being without delay, like the movement of your finger when a motive calls you to it and nothing stands in its way. These verses are a demonstration of how far they have gone astray and of the grave error of their disbelief in Allah, given the clarity of His signs that bear witness to Him, indicating His overwhelming power and His consummate wisdom, and that He is the one truly deserving to be worshipped, to be feared for His punishment, and to be hoped for in His reward in the abode of recompense.

And they will come forth before Allah (all together). [The verb is] expressed in the past tense, since what Allah, Mighty and Exalted, reports is, by virtue of its truth, as though it had already happened and taken place; and similar to this is "And the companions of Paradise will call out" and "And the companions of the Fire will call out," and their like.

The meaning of their coming forth before Allah—while nothing is hidden from Allah such that it would need to come forth before Him—is that they used to conceal themselves from eyes when committing indecencies, supposing that such things were hidden from Allah. Then, on the Day of Resurrection, they will be revealed before Allah in their own estimation, and they will know that nothing hidden is concealed from Him. Or [it means] they will come out of their graves and present themselves for the reckoning and judgment of Allah.

If you ask: why was "الضعفؤا" written with a waw before the hamza? I say: it was written according to the pronunciation of one who emphasizes the alif before the hamza, inclining it toward a waw. Its parallel is "علمؤا بنى إسرائيل" (the scholars of the Children of Israel).

Al-Du'afa' (the weak) are the followers and the common people. Al-Ladhina istakbaru (those who were arrogant) are their leaders and great ones, who led them astray, misled them, and turned them away from listening to the prophets and their followers.

Taba'an (as followers): plural of tabi' (follower) on the pattern of tabaʿ, like their saying khadim (servant) and khadam (servants), and ghaʾib (absent) and ghayb (absence). Or it is the plural of dhu tabaʿ (possessors of following). Tabaʿ means followers; one says "tabi'ahu tabaʿan" (he followed him).

If you ask: what is the difference between "min" in "min ʿadhab Allah" and its occurrence in "min shay'"? I say: the first is for specification (tabyin), and the second is for partitiveness (tab'id). It is as if it were said: "Will you relieve us of some of the thing which is the punishment of Allah?" It is also permissible that both are for partitiveness together, meaning: "Will you relieve us of some of a thing which is part of the punishment of Allah," i.e., some part of some part of the punishment of Allah.

If you ask: what is the meaning of their saying "Had Allah guided us, we would have guided you"? I say: what the weak said to them was a reproach to them and a rebuke for their having led them astray and misled them. Their saying "Will you relieve us at all of the punishment of Allah?" is by way of rebuke, since they knew that they would not be able to relieve them. So they answered them, offering an excuse for what had come from them toward them: that had Allah guided them to faith, they would have guided them and not misled them. This is either by attributing their sin in their misguidance and misleading to Allah (as Allah related about them, "Had Allah willed, we would not have associated, nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything," and "Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything apart from Him"), saying this in the Hereafter just as they used to say it in this world. This is confirmed by His statement, relating about the hypocrites: "On the Day when Allah raises them all up, they will swear to Him as they swear to you, and they think they are upon something."

Or the meaning is: "If we had been among the people of kindness, and our Lord had shown us kindness and we had been guided, we would have guided you to faith."

It was also said: its meaning is, "If Allah had guided us to the path of salvation from the punishment, we would have guided you," i.e., we would have relieved you and taken you along the path of salvation just as we took you along the path of destruction.

"Sawa'un ʿalayna a-jaziʿna am sabarna" (It is the same for us whether we bear it with impatience or with patience): the meanings are equal for us, impatience and patience. The hamza and "am" are for equalization. A similar example is: "Be patient or be not patient; it is the same for you," and the like.

It is reported that they will say: "Come, let us be impatient," so they will be impatient for five hundred years, and it will not benefit them; then they will say: "Come, let us be patient," so they will be patient in the same way, and then they will say: "It is the same for us."

If you ask: how is "It is the same for us" connected to what precedes it? I say: its connection to it is that their rebuke of them was impatience at what they were in. So they said: "It is the same for us whether we are impatient or patient," meaning themselves and them, since they are united in the punishment of the misguidance in which they were united. They are saying: "What is this impatience and rebuke? There is no benefit in impatience just as there is no benefit in patience, and the matter is more general than that."

Or, when they said "Had Allah guided us to the path of salvation, we would have relieved you and saved you," they followed it with despair of deliverance, saying: "We have no escape (mahis)," that is, no place of rescue or refuge, whether we are impatient or patient.

It is also permissible that this is from the speech of the weak and the arrogant together, as if it were said: "They all said: it is the same for us," like His statement: "That is so that he may know that I did not betray him."

The word "mahis" may be a verbal noun, like "maghib" and "mashib," and a noun of place, like "mabit" and "masif." It is said: "hasa ʿanhu" and "jada," with the same meaning.

As the matter was decided (*lamma qudiya al-amr*): it was cut off and finished, which is the reckoning, and the two groups were separated, one entering Paradise and the other entering the Fire. It is related that Satan will stand up at that time as an orator (*khatīban*) among the wretched of jinn and mankind, and will say: ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth﴾, which is resurrection and recompense for deeds; so He fulfilled for you what He promised. ﴿And I promised you, but I broke it for you﴾, meaning the opposite of that. ﴿And I had no authority over you﴾, meaning no power or domination, so as to compel you to disbelief and sins and force you into them, ﴿except that I called you﴾, meaning my calling you to misguidance through my whispering and beautifying it. The calling is not of the same kind as authority; it is like your saying: "Their greeting is nothing but beating." ﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾, for you were deceived by me and obeyed me when I called you, and you did not obey your Lord when He called you. This is evidence that man is the one who chooses wretchedness or happiness and brings it about for himself.

[[The phrase "the one who chooses wretchedness or happiness and brings it about for himself" is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school holding that man creates his own acts). The phrase "the Mujbirah" means Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah), and their doctrine is that Allah is the Creator of the causes of happiness and the causes of wretchedness, but the servant has acquisition (*kasb*) in them. From this, blame is directed at him, unlike the Mu'tazilah in their saying that the servant is the creator of them and brings them about for himself. Its verification is in the science of tawhid. (Ghayn)]] And there is nothing from Allah except enablement (*al-tamkīn*), and nothing from Satan except embellishment (*al-tazyīn*). Had the matter been as the Mujbirah claim, he would have said: "So do not blame me or yourselves, for Allah decreed disbelief upon you and compelled you to it."

If you say: "Satan's statement is false, and one may not rely on it." I say: If this statement of his were false, Allah would have made its falsehood clear and openly denied it. Moreover, there is no benefit for him in uttering falsehood in that situation. Do you not see his saying ﴿Indeed, Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I broke it for you﴾, how he brought in it truth and sincerity? And in his saying ﴿I had no authority over you﴾, it is like Allah's statement: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you among the misguided﴾ [15:42]. ﴿I am not one who will answer your cry for help, nor are you ones who will answer mine﴾, meaning neither of us will rescue the other from the punishment of Allah or relieve him. *Al-isrākh* means *al-ighātha* (rescue, relief). It is read *bi-muṣrikhiyya* with a kasra on the ya', which is weak, and they cited for it an anonymous verse:

*Qāla lahā: hal laki yā Tāfiyyi?*
*Qālat lahu: mā anta bi-l-mardiyyi*

*(He said to her: "Would you, O Tafi?"
She said to him: "You are not one to be pleased with.")*

*Its speaker is unknown. Tā is a demonstrative: i.e., "Would you, O woman, have a desire for...?" The original of the ya' of the first person is quiescence (sukūn). If it is vowelled, it is with fatḥa, but since here it met a quiescent letter before it, the ya', its kasra was permitted, according to the original rule for avoiding the meeting of two quiescent letters.*

*"Qālat" is a resumption (istinaf), as if it was said to him: "Then what did she say?" He said: "She said to him: 'You are not pleasing, for you are a man who presses on in every matter he resolves upon.'" So *māḍin* is the predicate of an omitted subject. The sentence is a resumptive answer to the question about the reason for not being pleased. He used the third-person pronoun in his saying "they" (*hum*), being parallel to the good. It is permissible to estimate the subject as the word "huwa" (he), in which case it is an *iltifāt* (shift) from address to the third person, indicating turning away from him, and mentioning the cause for another.*

It seems that he estimated the ya' of possession as quiescent with a quiescent ya' before it, so he vowelled it with a kasra according to the original rule for meeting two quiescent letters. But this is not correct, because the ya' of possession is only ever fatḥa when preceded by an alif, as in *ʿaṣāy* (my staff). So what about when it is preceded by a ya'? If you say: "The first ya' takes the course of a sound letter because of idghām (assimilation), so it is as if it were a ya' that came quiescent after a sound quiescent letter, so it was vowelled with a kasra according to the original," I say: This is a good analogy, but the widespread usage, which is like a mutawatir report, overrides analogies.

*Mā* in *bi-mā ashraktumūni* is a masdar-*mā* (verbal), and *min qabl* is connected to *ashraktumūnī*. The meaning: "I disbelieve today in your associating me [with Allah] from before this day," i.e., in the world, as in His saying ﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will disown your association﴾ [35:14]. The meaning of his disbelief in their association of him is his disassociation from it and his disapproval of it, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, we are free of you and of what you worship besides Allah; we have disbelieved in you﴾ [60:4]. It was also said: *min qabl* is connected to *kafartu* (I disbelieved).

*Mā* is a relative pronoun (*mawṣūla*), meaning: "I disbelieved before, when I refused to prostrate to Adam, in that which you associated with me, which is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic." You say "*sharaktu Zaydan*" (I made Zayd a partner); when you transfer it with the hamza, you say "*ashrakanīhi fulān*" (so-and-so made me a partner for him), i.e., made me a partner to him.

Similar to this *mā* is the *mā* in their saying: "Glory be to Him who subjected these to us" (*subḥāna mā sakhkharakunna lanā*). The meaning of their associating Satan with Allah is their obedience to him in what he used to beautify for them of worshipping idols and other things. This is the end of Iblis's speech. His saying ﴿Indeed, the wrongdoers﴾ is the statement of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is possible that it is part of Iblis's speech, and Allah, the Mighty and Exalted, only related what he would say at that time, so that it would be a kindness to the listeners in looking to their outcome and in preparing for what they must reach, and so that they would imagine in themselves that station at which Satan says what he says, so they would fear and act to free themselves from it and be saved.

It was also read *fa-lā yalūmūnī* with the ya' (third person), in the manner of *iltifāt*, as in His saying: ﴿until, when you are on the ship and they sail with them﴾ [10:22].

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 14, verse 23:

And al-Hasan and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd read: "wa-udkhila alladhina amanu" [and those who believed were made to enter], [[Mahmud said: "And al-Hasan and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd read: wa-udkhila alladhina amanu ʿala fiʿl al-mutakallim ... etc." Ahmad said:

If you ask: what turned al-Zamakhshari away from taking it as an iltifat (shift) from the first person to the third person, and compelled him to attach it to what follows, when he had room to do otherwise, and such a shift in this manner is common and widespread? Do you not see the words of God Most High: ﴿Ta Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched﴾ and then He said: ﴿A revelation from the One who created the earth﴾, and did not say "a revelation from Us"? I say: The discourse was turned away from this manner for a reason, namely that the apparent wording of udkhila in the first person indicates that their entry into Paradise was not through an intermediary but directly from God Most High, whereas the apparent meaning of the permission indicates attributing the entry to an intermediary, so there is a clash between them. But it seems good to me that it be attached to khalidin (abiding), and abiding is other than entering, so there is no clash. And God knows best.]] on the first-person verb, meaning: "And I cause them to enter." This is evidence that it is from the speech of God, not from the speech of Iblis. bi-idhni rabbihim [by the permission of their Lord] is connected to udkhila, that is:

The angels caused them to enter Paradise by the permission and command of God. If you say: then how is it connected in the other reading, and your saying "and I cause them to enter by the permission of their Lord" is an incoherent statement? I say: The correct way in this reading is that the phrase bi-idhni rabbihim be connected to what follows it, that is, ﴿their greeting therein will be "Peace"﴾ by the permission of their Lord, meaning: the angels greet them by the permission of their Lord.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 14, verses 24–25:

It is read as ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ﴾ with the ra' sukun (quiescent), just as ﴿من يتق﴾ is read [with the sukun], though this reading is weak. ﴿ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا﴾: "mathalan" is governed by and placed after "daraba" (he struck, i.e., set forth). ﴿وَكَلِمَةً طَيِّبَةً﴾ is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: He made a good word like a good tree. This is an explanation of His saying ﴿ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا﴾, like your saying: "The emir honored Zayd," meaning: he clothed him in a robe and mounted him on a horse.

It is also permissible for both "mathalan" and "kalimatan" to be in the accusative governed by "daraba," meaning: he struck a good word as an example, i.e., made it an example. Then He said ﴿كَشَجَرَةٍ طَيِّبَةٍ﴾ as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is like a good tree, ﴿أَصْلُهَا ثَابِتٌ﴾, i.e., in the earth, its roots striking firmly into it, ﴿وَفَرْعُهَا فِي السَّمَاءِ﴾, i.e., its height and its top are in the sky. It is also permissible that He intends "wa-furu'uha" (its branches), relying on the singular noun as a collective. Anas ibn Malik read: "kashajaratin tayyibatin thabitun asluha." If you ask: what is the difference between the two readings? I say: the reading of the majority is stronger in meaning, because in Anas's reading the attribute is applied to the tree; when you say "marartu bi-rajulin abuhu qa'imun" it is stronger in meaning than "marartu bi-rajulin qa'imin abuhu," because what is being predicated is the father, not the man.

The "good word" is the word of tawhid (monotheism). It was also said: every good word, such as tasbih (glorification), tahmid (praise), istighfar (seeking forgiveness), tawbah (repentance), and supplication. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas: the testimony that there is no god but Allah. As for the tree, every fruit-bearing tree with good fruit, such as the date palm, the fig tree, the grapevine, the pomegranate, and others.

It is reported from Ibn 'Umar that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said one day: "Indeed Allah has struck a parable of the believer: a tree. Tell me what it is." [Agreed upon; it has several wordings.] People began naming trees of the desert, and I was a boy, so it came into my heart that it was the date palm, but I was ashamed to say it since I was the youngest of the people. It is also reported: "What prevented me was that Abu Bakr and 'Umar were present, so I felt shy." 'Umar said to me: "O my son, if you had said it, it would have been dearer to me than red camels." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, it is the date palm."

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: it is a tree in Paradise.

His saying ﴿فِي السَّمَاءِ﴾ means in the direction of height and ascent; He does not mean a canopy. It is like your saying of a mountain: "tall in the sky," meaning its elevation and loftiness.

﴿تُؤْتِي أُكُلَهَا كُلَّ حِينٍ﴾: it gives its fruit at every time, at every season that God appoints for its bearing, ﴿بِإِذْنِ رَبِّهَا﴾, by the facilitation and creation of its Creator. ﴿لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ﴾: because in striking parables there is greater understanding, remembrance, and depiction of meanings.

Like an evil tree: its likeness is like the likeness of an evil tree. Read also: "wa-mathalu kalimatin" (and the likeness of an evil word) in the accusative, as a conjunction with "kalimatan tayyibatan" (a good word). The evil word is the word of shirk (associating partners with God). It is also said: every ugly word. As for the evil tree, it is every tree whose fruit is not good, such as the colocynth (al-Hanzal) and dodder (al-Kushut) [[His words "and dodder" (al-kushut): in al-Sihah, al-kushut is a plant that clings to the branches of trees without sending its roots into the earth.

The poet said:

"It is the dodder: no root, no leaf,
no fragrance, no shade, and no fruit."]] and the like. His words "uprooted from the surface of the earth" stand in contrast to His words "its root is firm." The meaning of "ujtutst" (it has been uprooted) is "istu'sisat" (it has been completely removed). The real sense of al-ijtithath is taking the whole trunk out. "Ma lahu min qarar" means: no stability. It is said: "qarra al-shay'u qararan," like your saying "thabata thabatan" (it remained firm). Likened to it is the saying that is not supported by proof, which is refuted and not firm; and that which does not endure either vanishes soon because it is false, from their saying: "al-batil lajlaj" (falsehood is slippery) [[His words "from their saying: al-batil lajlaj": in al-Sihah, "al-haqq abladj" (truth is clear), and "al-batil lajlaj," that is, it wavers without penetrating. (ʿa)]]. It is reported from Qatadah that someone said to one of the scholars: "What do you say about an evil word?" He replied: "I know of no place for it to settle on earth, nor any ascent for it in heaven, unless it clings to the neck of its speaker until he is brought with it to the Day of Resurrection."

with the firm word that is established by proof. The proof is in the heart of its holder and is firmly rooted in him, so he believes it and his soul is at rest in it. Their being made firm by it in this world: when they are tested in their religion they do not slip, as those whom the People of the Ditch tested stood firm, and those who were sawn apart with saws and whose flesh was combed off with iron combs, and as Jirjis and Shamsun and others stood firm. Their being made firm in the Hereafter: when they are questioned at the standing of witnesses about their belief and their religion, they do not stammer or become confused, and the terrors of the Gathering do not bewilder them. It was also said that its meaning is steadfastness at the questioning of the grave. On the authority of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the taking of the believer's soul and said: "Then his soul is returned to his body, and two angels come to him, make him sit up in his grave, and say to him: 'Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is your Prophet?' He says: 'My Lord is Allah, my religion is Islam, and my Prophet is Muhammad.' Then a caller calls from the heaven: 'My servant has spoken the truth.' That is His saying: Allah makes firm those who believe with the firm word."

[This is a portion of a long hadith narrated by Abu Dawud, Abu 'Awana, al-Hakim, Ahmad, Ibn Rahawayh, Ibn Abi Shayba and Abu Ya'la, from the narration of Sa'd ibn 'Ubayda, and in al-Bukhari as a marfu' report concerning His saying "Allah makes firm those who believe with the firm word": he said: it was revealed concerning the punishment of the grave. It is said to him: "Who is your Lord and who is your Prophet?" He says: "My Lord is Allah, and my Prophet is Muhammad (ﷺ)." That is His saying, exalted is He: "Allah makes firm those who believe..." to the end of the verse.]

And Allah leads astray the wrongdoers, those who did not hold to proof in their religion, but merely confined themselves to imitating their elders and their shaykhs, as the polytheists imitated their fathers, saying: "We found our fathers following a community" (43:23). Their being led astray in this world is that they do not stand firm at the times of trials, and their feet slip first of all; and in the Hereafter they are more misguided and more abased. "And Allah does what He wills" (14:27), that is, what wisdom requires, because the will of Allah follows wisdom: making believers firm and supporting them, preserving them when they remain steadfast and resolute, and leading the wrongdoers astray and forsaking them, leaving them to their own affairs when they slip.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 14, verses 28–30:

﴿Have you not considered those who exchanged the favour of Allah for ingratitude (kufr)...﴾ That is: they exchanged the thanks (shukr) for the favour of Allah for ingratitude (kufr), because the thanks for it which was obligatory upon them, they put in its place ingratitude. So it is as if they changed thanks into ingratitude and substituted it: ﴿exchanged﴾ (tabdil). Similar to this is ﴿and you make your provision that you deny (the truth)﴾, that is: the thanks for your provision, where you put denial in its place. Another interpretation: they exchanged the favour itself for ingratitude, in that when they denied it, it was taken from them, so they remained deprived of the favour, described by disbelief, with disbelief obtained by them in place of the favour. And they are the people of Makkah: Allah settled them in His sanctuary, made them the custodians of His House, and honoured them with Muhammad (ﷺ), but they denied the favour of Allah in place of the great thanks that was incumbent upon them. Or Allah bestowed upon them the favour in ease and abundance because of their journeys (of the two caravans, ﴿the caravans of winter and summer﴾), so they denied His favour, and He struck them with famine for seven years, so disbelief came to them in place of the favour. Likewise, when they were taken captive and killed on the day of Badr, the favour had departed from them and disbelief remained as a collar around their necks. And from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him): they are the two wicked ones of Quraysh: the Banu al-Mughirah and the Banu Umayyah. As for the Banu al-Mughirah, you (Muslims) sufficed against them on the day of Badr; and as for the Banu Umayyah, they were given enjoyment for a while.

It was said: they are the Christianized Arabs: Jabalah ibn al-Ayham and his companions. ﴿And they caused their people, who followed them in disbelief, to alight in the abode of destruction (dar al-bawar)﴾, that is: the abode of ruin. And ﴿Jahannam﴾ is in apposition (ʿatf bayan) to ﴿the abode of destruction﴾. It was read ﴿liyudillu﴾ with the yāʾ opened and with it dammed (i.e., both liyaḍillū and liyuḍillū).

If you say: misguidance and causing to go astray were not their aim in taking up rivals, so what is the meaning of the lām (of purpose)?

I say: since misguidance and causing misguidance were the result of taking up rivals, just as honouring was the result of coming in your saying "I came to you so that you honour me," the lām is brought in even though it is not the aim, by way of analogy and approximation. ﴿Enjoy yourselves (tamattaʿū)﴾ is a declaration that, because of their immersion in enjoying the present, and that they know no other and do not desire it, they are commanded to it: a commander obeyed has commanded them, whom they cannot oppose and who leave them no command of their own apart from it, and that is the command of appetite.

And the meaning: if you persist in what you are upon, in compliance with the command of appetite, then ﴿indeed your destination is the Fire﴾. It is permissible that what is meant is abandonment and leaving to oneself, and the like: ﴿Say: Enjoy your disbelief for a little while; indeed you are among the companions of the Fire.﴾

**The spoken words are omitted.** [[Mahmud said: "The spoken words are omitted..." etc.]] Ahmad said: There is a problem with this grammatical analysis (i'rab), because the answer would then be a report from God that if He told them this statement, they would comply with its requirement and establish the prayer and spend. But it has been said to them and many of them did not comply, and God's report is too exalted to be contradicted. This consideration is what leads many grammarians (mu'rabun) to turn away from this reading of the i'rab, since it occurs to them first from what has been mentioned. It can be made sound by understanding the general term as referring to the majority and not to all, and it is strengthened by two subtle points. The first: this construction is used only for those described as having true faith, whose faith is noted at the time of the command, like this verse, and like His saying ﴿And say to My servants that they should say that which is best﴾ [17:53], and ﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts; and say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts﴾ [24:30–31]. The second: it repeatedly comes for those described as "the servants of God," honored by their attribution to the Name of God, and they have said that the word "servants" in the Mighty Book is used only as praise of believers, especially when it is attributed to Him in an attribution of honor. The conclusion from this is that those commanded in these verses are people who are ready to comply and are in the realm of hastening to obedience, so the report about such people is true and correct, either as a general statement if that is intended, or as referring to the majority. And God knows best.

This is because the answer to "Say" (qul) indicates it, and its estimated form is: "Say to My servants who believe: establish the prayer and spend, they will establish the prayer and spend." They also allowed that "yuqimu" and "yunfiqu" could mean "liyuqimu" and "liyunfiqu" (in order that they establish and spend), and that this would be the spoken words. They said: The omission of the lam is permitted because the command "qul" stands in its place, and if one said "yuqimu al-salah wa yunfiqu" directly, without the lam, it would not be permitted.

If you ask: What is "sirran wa 'alaniyah" (secretly and openly) governed by? I say: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: "possessors of secrecy and openness," that is, "secretly and openly." Or it is in the accusative as a time adverb (zarf), meaning: "at times of secrecy and openness." Or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "spending in secret and spending openly." The meaning: concealing voluntary charity and making public the obligatory. And "al-khilal" means friendship (al-mukhalah).

If you ask: How does the command to spend correspond with the description of the day as one "in which there is no trading nor friendship"? [[His saying "in which there is no trading nor friendship": this reading is with the verb-ending on the fatha. (ʿ)]] I say: Because people give away their wealth in contracts of exchange, giving a return in order to receive its equivalent, and in acts of generosity and gifting to friends, in order to draw back with their gifts equivalents or better than them. But spending purely for the sake of God, as in His saying ﴿And none has a favor with him to be repaid, except the seeking of the countenance of his Lord, the Most High﴾ [92:19–20], is done only by sincere believers. So they were urged to do it in order to take its return on a day in which there is no trading nor friendship, that is, no benefit in trade or friendship, nor in what they spend of their wealth in exchanges and acts of generosity; benefit is gained there only from spending for the sake of God. It has also been recited as "lā bay'un fihi wa lā khilālun" with the nominative (raf').

Allah is the subject (mubtada'), and alladhi khalaqa (the One who created) is its predicate (khabar). "Min al-thamarat" (of the fruits) is an explanation (bayan) of "rizq" (provision), meaning: He brought forth by it provision which consists of fruits. It is also permissible for "min al-thamarat" to be the object (maf'ul) of "akhraja," with "rizqan" being a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the object, or an accusative of the verbal noun (masdar) of "akhraja," since it carries the sense of "rizq."

﴿By His command, and He has made subject to you the ships to run upon the sea﴾ — no, the commentary continues: "bi-amrihi" (by His command), by His saying "Be," ﴿and He has made subject to you the rivers﴾, ﴿and He has made subject to you the sun and the moon, both constant in their courses﴾, meaning they persevere in their motion, in giving light and in driving away darknesses, and in setting right what they set right of the earth, the bodies, and the plants. ﴿And He has made subject to you the night and the day﴾, alternating in succession (khilfah), for your livelihood and your rest [[Regarding his words "wa-subatakum": in al-Sihah, al-subat means sleep, and its origin is rest, and from it is the Exalted saying: ﴿And We made your sleep a rest (subat)﴾. (ʿ)]]. ﴿And He gave you of all that you asked Him for﴾ — "min" here is partitive (li-al-tab'id), meaning He gave you some of everything you asked for, considering your interests. It is recited "min kullin" with tanwin. "Ma sa'altumuhu" is a negation, and its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: He gave you of all that, without your having asked Him for it. It is also permissible for "ma" to be a relative pronoun (mawsulah), meaning: He gave you of all that which you needed, and your affairs and livelihoods would not have been set right without it; it is as if you had asked for it, or requested it through the tongue of your state. ﴿And if you tried to count the favours of Allah, you could not number them﴾, meaning you could not enumerate them or reach their end. This is when they wish to count them in summary; as for detail, none can manage it and none knows it except Allah. ﴿Indeed, man is surely a wrongdoer, a great ungrateful one﴾ — "wrongdoer" (zalum) means he wrongs the blessing by neglecting to give thanks for it; "ungrateful" (kaffar) means extremely ungrateful toward it.
