Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 14, verse 37:

"Part of my offspring" (مِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِي): some of my children, namely Isma'il and those descended from him, "in a valley" (بِوادٍ) which is the valley of Makkah, "without cultivation" (غَيْرِ ذِي زَرْعٍ): where there is never any crop at all. It is like His saying ﴿a Qur'an in Arabic, without any crookedness﴾ (قُرْآناً عَرَبِيًّا غَيْرَ ذِي عِوَجٍ), meaning there is no crookedness in it, nothing in it but straightness and nothing else.

It has been said that the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Muharram) is so called because God has made it forbidden to violate it and to treat it lightly, and He made the area around it a sanctuary (haram) because of its station. Or because it has always been a protected, mighty place, which every tyrant reveres, like a forbidden thing that must be avoided. Or because it is highly respected, of great sanctity, whose violation is not permitted. Or because He forbade the Flood from it, that is, prevented it from reaching it, just as it was named ʿAtiq because it was freed (ʿutiqa) from being seized by others.

"So that they may establish prayer" (لِيُقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ): the lam is connected to "I have settled" (أسكنت). That is: I did not settle them in this barren, desolate valley, lacking every source of livelihood and sustenance, except so that they might establish prayer at Your Sacred House, and make it flourish with the remembrance of You and worship of You, and with what Your mosques and places of worship are made flourishing by, seeking blessing from the spot You have honored above all other places, seeking happiness from Your noble neighbourhood, drawing near to You by devoting themselves at Your House, circumambulating it, and bowing and prostrating around it, seeking the descent of the mercy with which You have favored the inhabitants of Your sanctuary.

"Hearts of people" (أَفْئِدَةً مِنَ النَّاسِ): hearts from among the people. Here "min" is partitive (lil-tab'id), and this is supported by what is reported from Mujahid: "Had it said 'the hearts of people' (afidat al-nas), Persia and Byzantium would have crowded upon it." It has also been said: "Had it not said 'min', they would have crowded upon it, even the Byzantines, the Turks and the Indians."

It is also permissible that "min" be for the beginning of source (lil-ibtida'), as in your saying: "The heart from me is sick," meaning "my heart," so it is as if it were said: "hearts of people." The noun added to in this example is indefinite only because "hearts" (afidat) is indefinite in the verse, so that it encompasses some hearts.

It is read as "āfidah" (آفدة), on the pattern of "ʿāqidah." There are two possibilities in it: first, that it is from the heart (qalb), like your saying "ādar" for "adu'ar" (in the plural of "adr"). Second, that it is the active participle feminine of "afidat al-rihlah" when one hastens (in travel), meaning a group or groups who travel to them and hasten toward them.

It is also read as "afdah" (أفدة), and there are two possibilities: the hamzah is dropped for lightening, though the proper way to lighten it is by making it between-between (bayna bayna). And it may be from "afida," meaning "they swoop to them" (تَهْوِي إِلَيْهِمْ), they hasten toward them and fly toward them out of longing and yearning, from the verse:

*Whenever a pebble is thrown for him, you see him...*
*leaping at its fall like the leap of the young eagle* (ṭamūr al-akhyal)...

*And when he is woken from sleep, you see him*
*rising like a stick-shaped tuft, not a sluggard wrapped in his garments.*

*And when you cast him into the wide passes, you see him*
*swooping down the narrow paths like the swoop of the falcon.*

*And when you look at the lines of his face,*
*they shine like the flash of a lightning cloud.*

These are by Abu Kabir al-Hudhali, describing Ta'abbata Sharran in alertness and courage. He says: when you throw a pebble at him to test whether he is asleep or awake, he leaps quickly (yanzū, "leaps"); ṭamūr al-akhyal means the leap of the akhyal, that is, rising as it rises, the akhyal being a bird from which the Arabs take omens; its root is from takhayyul (imagination) or possibly from khuyala (vanity). Rattaba rutūban means he stood upright and rose high, that is: you see him rising from the ground like the rising of the ankle-bone (kaʿb al-sāq). Al-zamal, al-zamāl and al-zamīl (with the mīm doubled in each) is the weak one wrapped in his clothes. Then he says: when you hurl him into the wide open places, you see him swooping down its narrow paths, that is, he hastens along its narrow tracks, like the swoop of the ajdal, which is the falcon, that is, like its speed in flight. It is also reported as "al-jandal," meaning the stone. Al-asarah are the lines of the forehead, plural of sarar. Al-ʿāriḍ is the cloud spread across the horizon, and al-mutahallil is the shining one, or the high one about to rain.

It is reported from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "I was sitting spinning yarn in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was mending his sandal, and the sweat of his brow shone like light, and a light was born in my eyes, so I began looking at him. He said: 'What are you looking at?' I told him that, and said: 'By Allah, if the Hudhali saw you, he would know that you are more worthy of his poetry.' He said: 'And what did he say?' I said: 'And when you look...' (the verse). Then he put down what was in his hand, stood up, kissed between my eyes and said: 'May Allah reward you with good. I have never been as delighted as I am by your words.'"

It is also read "tahwī ilayhim" (تهوى إليهم) in the passive form, from "hawā ilayhi" and "ahwāhu ghayruhu" (someone else made it fall). And "tahwī ilayhim" from "hawā yahwā" when one loves, its meaning being embedded with the sense of "tanzaʿu" (yearns), so it takes its construction.

"And provide them with fruits" (وَارْزُقْهُمْ مِنَ الثَّمَراتِ), despite their dwelling in a valley with none of them, by having them brought to them from the lands, "so that they may give thanks" (لَعَلَّهُمْ يَشْكُرُونَ), for the blessing that varieties of fruits be provided to them present in a desolate valley, a wasteland without herbage (najm), without trees and without water. There is no doubt that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, answered his prayer, made it a sanctuary, safe, to which the fruits of everything are brought as provision from His presence. Then He favored it in the existence of kinds of fruit within it over every fertile land and over the most fertile and abundant in fruit of lands, and in whatever land of East or West you see the marvel that Allah shows you in a valley without cultivation, which is the gathering together of early and varied fruits of spring, summer and autumn in a single day. This is not strange among His signs. May Allah grant us enjoyment of dwelling in His sanctuary, enable us to give thanks for His blessings, keep us honored by entering under the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and grant us a portion of the soundness of that sound heart.

The repeated address is evidence of humble supplication and seeking refuge in God, Exalted.

﴿Indeed, You know what we conceal and what we reveal.﴾ He knows the secret as He knows the open, with knowledge that admits no variation, because no unseen thing is hidden from Him. The meaning is: You are more knowing of our circumstances, and of what benefits us and what harms us, than we are ourselves; You are more merciful to us and more sincere toward us than we are toward ourselves. So there is no need for supplication and request; we call upon You only to manifest servitude to You, to show humility before Your greatness, to abase ourselves before Your might, to express our need for what is with You, to hasten to receive Your favours, and to long for Your mercy. It is like a servant ingratiating himself before his master, desiring to obtain his kindness, while the master is fully able and of good disposition.

It is related from some of them that he raised his need to a generous person, but the granting was delayed, so he wished to remind him, saying: "One like you is not to be reminded," out of regarding him as neglectful or as forgetful of the needs of those who ask; but the one with a need is not restrained by his need from speaking about it.

It was said: what we conceal is the inner grief caused by the separation that has occurred between us, and what we reveal is the weeping and the supplication. It was also said: what we conceal is the sorrow of parting, and what we reveal is:

He means what passed between him and Hajar when she said to him at the farewell: "To whom are You leaving us?" He said: "To God I entrust you." She said: "Did God command you this?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Then we shall not fear; You have left us to One who suffices."

﴿And nothing is hidden from God﴾ is either the words of God, Mighty and Majestic, confirming Ibrahim (upon him peace), like His saying ﴿And thus they do﴾, or the words of Ibrahim, meaning: nothing among things is hidden from God, who is the Knower of the unseen, in every place. "Min" (from/any) is for totality, as if it were said: nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him.

"ʿAlā" in His saying ﴿in old age﴾ means "with" (maʿa), like the poet's words:

"Despite what you see of my old age, I know from where the shoulder is eaten."

[Tara'īn: its origin is tara'yīn, in the pattern of tafʿalīn; the fatha of the hamza was moved to the rāʾ, then it was deleted, and the first yāʾ was deleted after being converted to an alif because it moved and the letter before it was open. He says: I, despite what you look upon of my old age and decrepitude which normally causes senility, am knowing of matters and alert to them. He alluded to this by his words "I know from where the shoulder is eaten," meaning: I know the answer to this question. It is also narrated as "from where" (min ḥaythu), so perhaps "min" is extra. Some said: the shoulder is eaten from its lower part, and its eating is hard from its upper part, and it is a proverb struck for the experienced one who is alert to affairs.]

It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: grant me, while I am old and in a state of old age. It is related that Ismaʿil was born to him when he was ninety-nine years old, and Ishaq was born to him when he was one hundred and twelve years old; and it is also related that Ismaʿil was born to him at sixty-four, and Ishaq at ninety. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: no child was born to Ibrahim except after one hundred and seventeen years. He mentioned the state of old age because the favour of granting a child is greater in such a state, in that it is a time when despair of childbearing has set in, and attaining one's need after despair is among the most noble and sweetest of blessings in the soul of the one who attains it. Moreover, the birth at that advanced age was a sign for Ibrahim.

﴿Indeed, my Lord is All-Hearer of supplication﴾: he had called upon his Lord and asked for a child, saying: "My Lord, grant me of the righteous," so he thanked God for what He had honoured him with by answering him. If you say: God hears every supplication, whether He answers it or not? I say: it is from your saying "the king heard the words of so-and-so" when he took them into account and accepted them. From it: "God hears whoever praises Him." In the hadith [Agreed upon, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with him]: "God has given permission to nothing as He gives permission to a prophet who chants the Qur'an beautifully" [Its wording "like His permission to a prophet who chants the Qur'an" is in al-Sihah as "like His permission to one who chants..." (ʿ)]. If you say: what is this, the attribution of "All-Hearer" to "supplication"? I say: it is the attribution of the attribute to its object, and its original form is "All-Hearer of supplication." Sibawayh mentioned faʿīl among the intensive patterns that work as verbs, as in your saying: "this one strikes Zayd (ḍarūb Zaydan), and striker of his brother (ḍarrāb akhāhu), slaughterer of his camels (mināḥar ibilihi), one who is wary of matters (ḥadhar umūran), and merciful to his father (raḥīm abāhu)." It may also be that it is the attribution of faʿīl to its doer, and making God's supplication "hearer" by metaphorical attribution.

The intended meaning is God's hearing.

The intended meaning is God's hearing.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 14, verses 42–43:

If you say: God is exalted above forgetfulness and heedlessness, so how could the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who knows Him better than anyone, think that He is heedless, to the point that it was said, ﴿And do not think that God is heedless﴾? I answer: If the address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), there are two interpretations. The first is to confirm him in what he already was, namely that he did not think God was heedless, like His saying, ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾, and ﴿And do not call upon another god besides God﴾, just as in the command, ﴿O you who have believed, believe in God and His Messenger﴾. The second is that the prohibition against thinking Him heedless is intended as an announcement that He knows what the wrongdoers do, that nothing of it is hidden from Him, and that He will punish them for its little and its much by way of warning and threat, like His saying, ﴿And God is Knowing of what you do﴾, meaning a threat. It is also permissible to mean: do not think that He deals with them as one who is heedless of what they do, but as one who watches over them and reckons with them for the smallest speck and the tiniest thing. If the address is to someone else, one who might think Him heedless because of ignorance of His attributes, then there is no question about it.

It is related from Ibn 'Uyayna: "It is a consolation to the wronged and a threat to the wrongdoer." He was asked, "Who said this?" He became angry and said, "He said it from his own knowledge."

It was recited, "yu'akhkhiruhum" (He delays them), with the nun and with the ya'. ﴿Wherein the eyes will be fixed﴾, meaning their eyes will not stay in their places because of the terror of what they see. ﴿Racing forward, with heads raised﴾: racing toward the caller. It was said: ihtaa' (ihṭā', fixed gazing) is that you turn your eye upon the thing seen and keep looking at it without blinking. ﴿Their heads raised﴾: lifting them. ﴿Their glance will not return to them﴾: it will not come back to them so that they blink with their eyes; that is, they do not blink, but their eyes are open and wide without moving the eyelids. Or: their sight does not return to them so that they look at themselves.

Hawa' (hawāʾ, emptiness): the void that is not occupied by bodies. From it comes the expression, "So-and-so's heart is hawa'," when he is a coward with no strength or courage in his heart. It is also said of a fool: "his heart is hawa'." Zuhayr said:

"Like the ostriches, whose breast is hollow (hawa')
As though the saddle on her was over a bald-headed, small-headed she-camel..."

(The lines describe Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma's camel.) Ṣa'l means one whose hair on the head is bare and whose head is small. Ẓulmān is the plural of ẓalīm, which is the young ostrich. Ju'ju' means the chest. Hawā' means empty and vacant, and he made its chest empty so that it would be quicker in running to its food. Aṣak is one whose knees knock together when walking because of the length of his legs. Ṣallama means he cut it off; taslim is an intensive form. It is said: ajnā the fruit when it ripened, and ajnat the earth when its herbage and its plants increased. As-Sinn is a level place and the name of a specific place. At-tanūm, on the pattern of tannūr, is a tree whose sheath splits open to reveal small seeds eaten by desert people, its colour tending toward black; it is said to be the shahdanaj tree. Al-ā' is a kind of tree whose single unit is āʾa. It is also said that its fruit is called by this name, and it is applied to a kind of sound. At-tanūm is the subject of ajnā, meaning that these two kinds became abundant in that place.

Because the ostrich is a proverb for cowardice and foolishness. Hassan said:

"Let me inform Abu Sufyan on my behalf:
You are hollow-bodied, empty-hearted (hawāʾ).
Our swords left slaves,
and the women are the masters of the Abd al-Dar clan.
You satirized Muhammad, and I answered on his behalf,
and with God is the reward for that.
Do you satirize him, when you are not his equal?
So may the worst of you ransom the best of you.
Is the one among you who satirizes the Messenger of God
equal to the one who praises him and supports him?
If he refuses, and his father and my honour
are a shield for the honour of Muhammad against you."

Hassan composed this satirizing Abu Sufyan before his conversion to Islam. Alā is a particle of alerting. The one addressed in "bilāgh" (to convey) is not specified, and the expected wording would have been "fa-innahu" (that he), meaning Abu Sufyan, but he addressed him with the reproach because it is more enraging. It is also permissible that the one commanded is Abu Sufyan himself, so he is a vocative with the particle of calling omitted.

Al-mujawwaf, al-nakhab and al-hawā' mean empty of the belly, or empty of heart in respect of reason and courage. In another version, instead of this half-line, it is related: "mughalghala, then the concealment has departed (barah al-khafā')". Mughalghala means heated, from ghulla (with a ḍamma), which is intense thirst and heat. It is also said: transmitted from one place to another. Barah, like sami'a, means departed and vanished. It is also said: became manifest and clear, from barāḥ al-arḍ, which is its open part, so khafā' means concealment or secrecy.

The attribution of leaving to the swords is a figurative attribution in the mind (majāz ʿaqlī), because they are the instrument of the act. ʿUbayd, with diminutive form, is a tribe, and likewise ʿAbd al-Dār. Sādatuhā is the subject (mubtadaʾ). Al-imāʾ is its predicate (khabar), and the clause is in the position of the second object of tarakat (left), meaning they made them slaves with no masters except women, and they made the clan of ʿAbd al-Dār like that. He means that we annihilated their men, the leaders and the nobles, so their nobles are only women, and indeed it is permissible that they are, besides the free women, all the same, so only the female slaves remain. "Wa-atahjūhu" is a reproachful interrogative, and the wāw after it is for the circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: that is not fitting. Sharr and khayr (worst and best) are of the form of the comparative (afʿal al-tafḍīl), and both are used with the hamza dropped for lightness because of their frequent use, but what is meant here is the basic quality of the attribute, not an increase in it. Al-sharr is Abu Sufyan. The clause is supplicatory: he prayed against him that he would be a ransom for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). He presented it in the form of vagueness for the sake of fairness in speech, and for this reason, when those present heard it, they said, "This is half a line which the Arabs have said, so be fair." "Amman yahjūhu" is an interrogative of denial, meaning that the one among you who satirizes him and the one among us who praises him and supports him are not equal. It is possible that the hamza is for alerting, or for calling, and the vocative is omitted, meaning: O people of Abu Sufyan, the one among you who satirizes the Messenger of God and the one among you who praises him and supports him are equal in not being bothered by either. It is related: "faman" (whoever), and there must be an assumed element: whoever among you satirizes him and forsakes him, so that forsaking is matched with support, like satire with praise. Moreover, in this there is evidence for the permissibility of omitting the relative pronoun (al-mawṣūl), which the Kufans and al-Akhfash permitted, and Abu Malik followed them, but he made a condition that it be coordinated with another relative pronoun, as here. His saying "wa-wālidahu" means the father of my mother. It is related: "wa-wālidatī" (and my mother). Al-wiqāʾ is that by which one protects against what is disliked, like a shield; its pattern is that of al-ḥizām and al-ribāṭ, for the object of the verb, so it is either in the sense of the passive participle or of the instrument. I saw in al-Zamakhshari's words what indicates naming this pattern as the passive participle. In al-Hamʿ there is what indicates that it came irregularly among the patterns of the instrument, like irāth, that by which fire is kindled, meaning set alight, and sirād, that by which something is stitched, meaning cut.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) heard his saying, "And with God is the reward for that," he said: "May God reward you with Paradise for your good." When he heard his saying, "If he refuses," he said: "And God says: the heat of the Fire is good (for you)." His approval of the retaliation with reproach indicates that it is permissible.

It is related from Ibn Jurayj: ﴿Their hearts are hawāʾ﴾, empty of good, void of it. Abu ʿUbayda said: hollow, having no minds.

The day the punishment comes to them: this is the second object of *anzir* (warn), and it refers to the Day of Resurrection. The meaning of *akhkhirna ila ajalin qarib* ("delay us to a near term") is: return us to the world and grant us respite until a near limit of time, so that we may make up for what we neglected of answering your call and following your messengers. Or the "day" may be understood as the day of their destruction by swift punishment, or the day of their death, when they are tormented by the severity of the death agonies and meet the angels without good tidings. They will ask on that day that their Lord delay them to a near term, like His saying: "Why did You not delay me to a near term, so that I would give charity and be among the righteous?"

*Awa lam takunu aqsamtum* ("Did you not swear"): this is in the sense of intending to say. There are two aspects to it: that they say this out of insolence and arrogance, and because ignorance and foolishness had taken hold of them; and that they say it through the tongue of their state, since they built sturdy structures and entertained far-reaching hopes. *Ma lakum* ("you have no") is the answer to the oath. It came in the form of direct address because of *aqsamtum* ("you swore"). Had the words of the swearers been quoted directly, it would have said: *ma lana min zawal* ("we have no cessation"). **The Day the earth will be changed into a different earth** is in the accusative as a substitution (*badal*) for "the day it comes to them," or as an adverbial (*zarf*) governed by "retribution."

The meaning is: on the day this earth you know is changed into another earth, unlike this known one, and likewise the heavens. *Tabdil* (substitution) means change. It may apply to the essences themselves, as when you say, "I exchanged the dirhams for dinars." From this is the Qur'anic statement ﴿We will replace them with other skins﴾ and ﴿We will replace their two gardens with two gardens﴾. It may also apply to attributes, as when you say, "I made the ring into a seal," meaning you melted the ring and shaped it into a seal, transferring it from one form to another. From this is the statement of God, exalted be He, ﴿Those—God will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾.

Scholars differ concerning the change of the earth and the heavens. It has been said that their attributes will change: the mountains will be removed from the earth, its seas will be made to burst forth, and it will be leveled so that no crookedness or elevation is seen in it. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is the same earth, but it will merely be altered. He recited:

*And the people are not the people you knew,*
*nor is the abode the abode you used to know.*

[[He means: the people today are not the people you knew before, since the living among them have perished, and the abode today is not the abode you used to know, since its conditions have changed and its attributes have been altered.]]

The heaven will be changed by the scattering of its stars, the eclipse of its sun, the darkening of its moon, its splitting open, and its becoming gates.

It has also been said that another earth and other heavens will be created in its place. It is reported from Ibn Masʿud and Anas that people will be gathered upon a white earth on which no one has committed a sin. It is reported from ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, that the earth will be changed into silver and the heavens into gold.

It is reported from al-Dahhak: a white silver earth like scrolls. It was also read: ﴿the day We change the earth,﴾ with the nun.

[[His statement "and it was read: 'We change the earth' with the nun" is perhaps "and 'the earth and the heavens' in the accusative, so let it be verified. The recitation. (ʿ)"]]

It is God's, the One, the Subduer﴾, because when dominion belongs to one who overpowers and cannot be overpowered or resisted, then no one has anyone to appeal to besides Him or seek refuge with, and the matter is at the utmost difficulty and severity.

﴿Bound together﴾: bound with one another, or with the devils.

Or: their hands are bound to their feet, shackled. His statement ﴿in fetters﴾ may be connected to "bound together," meaning they are bound together in fetters; or it may not be connected to it, in which case the meaning is: bound together and manacled. *Al-asfad* (fetters) means chains. It has been said they are shackles. He recited, for Salama ibn Jandal:

*Zayd al-Khayl has met with shackles,*
*biting with a forearm and a shin-bone.*

[[By Salama ibn Jandal. Zayd al-Khayl is the one whom the Prophet ﷺ named Zayd al-Khayr. "Has met": he obtained from his enemies shackles, meaning chains and fetters. **Qatran** (tar) has three dialects: *qatran*, *qitran*, and *qatran* with the qaf vowelled differently, with the ta' sukun. It is what drips from a tree called *al-abhal*, which is boiled, and mangy camels are smeared with it, so the mange is burned away by its heat and sharpness, as is the skin. Its heat may reach the belly. Its nature is that fire ignites quickly in it, and it may be used as a lamp fuel. It is black in color and foul in smell. The skins of the people of the Fire will be smeared with it until its coating becomes for them like *sarabil*, which are shirts, so that four things gather upon them: the sting of the tar, its burning, the rapid spread of the fire through their skins, the ugly color, and the stench.
